stories.title_zh: 澳大利亚数据中心创始人披露IPO前债务攀升
stories.content:
*London* | Australian-helmed data centre provider Nscale needs much more cash to meet current contracts and has piled on more debt, but still plans to proceed with a listing in New York, an updated prospectus shows.

Nscale also revealed it has deeper ties than previously disclosed to scandal-hit Nvidia, a stakeholder and critical supplier of chips for its AI data centres. The chip giant has committed $US2 billion ($2.95 billion) of Nscale’s more than $US3 billion in convertible financing agreed to in September, $US1 billion more than first disclosed.

NextDC data centre builder Kapitol Group is looking for other sources of work as popular opposition to the digital warehouses grows, policymakers consider tighter rules for new facilities and developer clients increasingly put planned projects on hold.

Melbourne-based Kapitol, an eight-year-old contractor that has grown rapidly on the back of work for clients including NextDC to become one of the country’s largest, is expanding into Queensland from its Melbourne base to tap the demand for construction in housing and infrastructure.

stories.title: Digital Realty Trust to spend $10bn more on Japan data centers: CEO
stories.summary: Digital Realty Trust plans to invest an additional $10 billion in Japanese data center development beyond its existing commitments, according to CEO Andy Power, as the REIT capitalizes on Tokyo and Osaka's emergence as critical nodes for Asia-Pacific cloud and AI traffic. The expanded capital deployment reflects sustained confidence in Japan's stable regulatory environment and proximity to major Asian markets despite domestic land and power constraints.
stories.why_it_matters: The $10 billion increment intensifies competition for scarce Tokyo-Osaka land and grid interconnection points, likely accelerating land banking by local developers and pushing secondary markets like Fukuoka and Sapporo into consideration. Japanese utilities face pressure to reform wholesale power markets as foreign operators with long-term capital undercut domestic colocation providers unable to match similar renewable energy commitments.

stories.why_zh: 这100亿美元的增量加剧了东京-大阪稀缺土地和电网互联点的竞争，可能加速本地开发商的土地储备，并推动福冈和札幌等次级市场进入考虑范围。日本公用事业公司面临改革批发电力市场的压力，因为拥有长期资本的外国运营商削弱了无法匹配类似可再生能源承诺的国内colocation供应商。

stories.title: AI chips, rare earths and trade: 5 US-China questions looming over Shenzhen APEC CEO summit
stories.summary: Observers have low expectations for big changes
stories.title_zh: AI chips、稀土与贸易：深圳APEC CEO峰会上悬而未决的5个中美问题
stories.content:
Observers have low expectations for big changes

US-CHINESE business relations were thrown a curveball ahead of a major CEO summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov 17 and 18. On Thursday (Nov 12), Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia after it was revealed that he had affairs with an executive at the company and a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

One of the architects of the artificial intelligence boom, Huang was also perhaps the strongest proponent in Washington for US companies selling AI hardware to China – an issue that has become central to the countries’ fraught economic relationship. Huang, who has a close relationship with US President Donald Trump, has also promoted open AI models, an approach favoured by many Chinese firms.

China hawks in Congress have already seized on the scandal, using it to push for three Bills that would put more restrictions on technology exports to the country.

Next week’s summit, which is hosted by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum, has the potential to advance policy talks. Trump and the Chinese leader Xi Jinping (and perhaps President Vladimir Putin of Russia) are expected to meet. On the sidelines, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will take part in a bilateral dialogue on AI.

But observers have low expectations for big changes. “The Chinese would like to prolong this fragile stability for as long as they can,” Ryan Hass, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who advised President Barack Obama and White House officials on US policy toward China, told *The New York Times*.

Still, amid a stalled trade war, expanding export controls, legal tussles and suspected spy games, the conversation may have just gotten a little more complicated. Here are the biggest questions looming about the world’s most important economic relationship.

## 1. Does America clamp down further on the export of advanced chips?

The US has banned its most advanced AI chips, like Nvidia’s Blackwell, from reaching China – though, given reports of chip smuggling operations in Singapore, Taiwan and elsewhere, perhaps to limited effect.

In designing and manufacturing advanced semiconductors, China’s capabilities still lag those of the US and Taiwan. Hawks want to keep it that way. But Trump has been less than resolute. In January, his administration allowed sales of Nvidia’s less powerful H200 to China, a move that is now being scrutinised by Congress in the wake of Huang’s resignation.

On Capitol Hill, a handful of proposed pieces of legislation could severely restrict China’s access. “Given how vocal Congress has been on this topic, and given the fact that Congress is going to be more empowered post-midterms, it’s less likely we get a loosening of chip rules and more likely we get a tightening,” said Chris Miller, author of *Chip War: The Fight for the World’s Most Critical Technology*.

On the other side of the chip coin are foreign data centres, which have largely escaped Washington’s attention. That may soon change, too. Lawmakers in Congress have been pushing for tighter limits on Chinese companies’ renting computing power abroad, whether from US-owned data centres or facilities running American chips.

In November, the US firm Oracle cancelled a roughly US$7 billion contract that gave Tencent, a Chinese company, access to advanced AI chips in data centres in South-east Asia, after US officials raised concerns, according to *The Financial Times*.

In 2027, US cloud giants like Microsoft and Amazon could face similar scrutiny for hosting open-weight models from Chinese labs such as Moonshot and Z.ai, said Paul Triolo, partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, a global advisory firm.

If the US further restricts access to chips, China would probably retaliate by restricting access to rare earths and the powerful magnets made from them, which go into products as varied as electric vehicles and fighter jets. “We’re sort of on the brink here,” Triolo said. “If the Chinese escalate further on rare-earths export controls, we’re in uncharted territory.”

## 2. Does China further barricade its tech economy?

In Shenzhen, US tech executives will probably press for more leniency for their companies in China. On the whole, observers said, they are unlikely to get it.

In May, Bloomberg reported that China had begun requiring senior AI researchers and executives at private firms like Alibaba and DeepSeek to get approval before travelling abroad, with some surrendering their passports.

The authorities also barred the two Chinese founders of Manus, an AI startup based in Singapore, from leaving China after the company was acquired by Meta, then ordered Meta to unwind the deal.

In November, Chinese regulators blocked SoftBank’s US$5.4 billion acquisition of a robotics firm on national security grounds. And China’s own export control list – which includes not just rare earths but also batteries and industrial machinery related to solar panels and tunnel boring – is lengthening.

## 3. Can America make progress on rare earths?

China dominates the market for rare earths. In 2025, Beijing responded to US tariffs and semiconductor controls with a series of sweeping export restrictions on these elements, which forced the Trump administration to back down.

US policymakers have since scrambled to erode that dependence. So far, more than US$2.5 billion in federal loans and equity has flowed into American rare earth companies like MP Materials, which operates the country’s only producing rare earth mine, and USA Rare Earth, which is building a mine-to-magnet supply chain in Texas and Oklahoma.

Washington is also striking mining deals abroad, in Australia, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and elsewhere. Still, experts said such efforts would take years to bear fruit.

“Until new rare-earths processing facilities and permanent magnet manufacturing capabilities come online, it will continue to feature as a bargaining tool by the Chinese,” said Gracelin Baskaran, a director of the Critical Minerals Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

## 4. Does the trade war truce hold long term or disintegrate?

In April 2025, after “Liberation Day” set off a tit-for-tat escalation with Beijing, tariffs on Chinese goods reached as high as 145 per cent. A month later, after bilateral talks in Geneva, those fell to 30 per cent. In October 2025, on the sidelines of an Apec summit in Busan, South Korea, Trump and Xi struck a truce. Washington agreed to lower the rate further while Beijing paused its rare-earth export controls and agreed to buy American agricultural products and Boeing jets.

China, according to industry observers, has not followed through on its promises. In November, the White House voiced its displeasure with Beijing, a move officials might reiterate in Shenzhen. On Jan 10, 2027, the Busan agreement is set to expire. Instead of extending it, the Trump administration may take new offensive measures, such as financial sanctions against Chinese companies.

“The current US-China detente could come apart,” Doshi said.

In 2027, the trade war could resume in earnest. Would that mean decoupling continues? This year, American exports to China barely recovered from a 26 per cent plunge in 2025, the steepest in recent history.

Chinese exports to the US were down about 11 per cent through September, though they have been climbing since the spring, as China’s global trade surplus surpassed US$1 trillion. Washington has also continued to restrict Chinese technology. Still, Bessent said this week that Washington’s intent is to “de-risk, not to decouple” with China.

In September, the countries announced a 30-for-30 deal: China would lower barriers on US$30 billion of US exports, and the US would lower barriers on US$30 billion of Chinese imports. The sides have exchanged product lists, but the deal still awaits domestic legal confirmation.

## 5. Does a black swan take flight?

Some years ago, Xi ordered his military forces to be ready for a successful invasion of Taiwan by 2027. The Chinese leader will be 74 next year and presumably contemplating his legacy. With a new term likely beginning and a Trump presidency waning, will he give the order? Or will a conflict finally erupt over contested territories in the South China Sea? A great power war is the blackest of black swans.

But there is also the potential for an AI-enabled cyberattack that wreaks havoc in either China or the US, Triolo said. Or the semiconductor market could implode in some way, Miller added. As Xi warned Communist Party cadres in October, “Be ready at all times to withstand the major tests of high winds, choppy waters and even stormy seas.” NYTIMES

stories.title: Eclypsium spotlights AI hardware attack blind spot
stories.summary: Researchers have shown a compromised DPU can change AI outputs in memory, exposing gaps in checks that only verify saved model files.
stories.content:
Sat, 14th Nov 2026 (Today)
Eclypsium has published research on attacks that can alter the behaviour of AI models through the hardware they run on, with support from NVIDIA.

The findings focus on risks in AI data centre infrastructure rather than in model files or application layers.

In a controlled demonstration, attackers with privileged access to underlying systems were able to manipulate a model while it was running without changing the original model files or triggering traditional integrity checks. The research described a scenario in which a compromised DPU, combined with permissive memory isolation, modified model weights directly in memory.

This could allow an attacker to influence outputs during live inference while leaving stored models unchanged. Eclypsium said this exposes a gap between checks that confirm whether a saved model has been altered and how that model behaves once it is executed on complex hardware.

### Blind spot

The study adds to a wider debate over where AI security efforts are focused as companies and public bodies roll out systems at speed. Much of the current discussion around AI safety has centred on training data, model behaviour, guardrails and governance, while the servers, firmware, networking components and supply chains behind those systems have received less attention.

Eclypsium argues that this creates what it calls an "AI Infrastructure Assurance Gap", in which an organisation may trust a model because the file passes integrity checks even though the underlying infrastructure has been tampered with. In the demonstration, the manipulated model produced changed analytical output in response to a real-world geopolitical query.

Eclypsium is working with NVIDIA on infrastructure assurance through integration with the Open Agent Safety Platform. The collaboration is intended to support independent verification and continuous monitoring of the systems used to train and run AI models and agents.

The issue has commercial significance because spending on AI infrastructure is rising sharply. Goldman Sachs has forecast that global investment in AI infrastructure will exceed USD $1 trillion annually in 2026, while the World Economic Forum has cited estimates that AI could contribute USD $15.7 trillion to global GDP.

### Attack path

The technical findings described an attack chain targeting a privileged part of AI compute infrastructure that enabled compromise of a model, including its weights. According to Eclypsium, the technique made it possible to alter model output during live inference without modifying the stored model or the inference service, and without visible indicators of compromise.

This matters because many existing security controls are designed to verify software artefacts, configurations or access permissions rather than the integrity of every hardware and firmware layer involved in execution. In practice, a model could appear unchanged to standard checks while producing manipulated answers.

"AI security starts with trusting the infrastructure that it runs on. Our research demonstrates how hardware-level compromises can undermine AI execution without being detected by the stored-model integrity checks used in the demonstration. Through Eclypsium's independent verification and continuous monitoring, we're helping organizations establish and maintain trust in the infrastructure powering AI," said Yuriy Bulygin, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder, Eclypsium.

NVIDIA described the work as part of a broader effort to improve protections around AI systems. The chipmaker has become central to the market for AI hardware, so the focus on infrastructure trust extends beyond one supplier to the wider ecosystem of accelerators, networking equipment, firmware and supporting components used in AI data centres.

"NVIDIA builds security into its platforms to help customers protect their AI infrastructure. Working with researchers and cybersecurity companies, like Eclypsium, we're continuously strengthening protections across the AI ecosystem," said Gilad Shainer, Senior Vice President of Networking, NVIDIA.

### Independent checks

Outside experts quoted alongside the research said the findings point to a need for stronger independent validation of AI infrastructure. The concern is that increasingly complex systems are being used in settings where AI outputs could shape significant operational or policy decisions.

"Some of the most consequential and complex decision systems ever are being developed now. The new architectures that AI systems are running on, because of their complexity and speed, benefit from independent verification. AI infrastructure should be treated as critical infrastructure, with verifiable evidence that it is in a known-good state. Securing critical infrastructure is a team sport, and this is a successful example of how to do it: researchers demonstrated an attack scenario and worked with the manufacturer to help clarify practical protections that the whole industry can use," said Jon Rolf, Cybersecurity Consultant, Rolf Cyber.

Others said transparency practices used in software security need to extend more fully into firmware and hardware, particularly in AI environments where organisations may depend on long and opaque supply chains.

"This research reinforces the need for full-stack transparency and monitoring across AI infrastructure. Organisations can't secure what they can't see, and the same transparency standards applied to software must extend to firmware and hardware. A Bill of Materials is just the beginning. AI infrastructure needs to turn this transparency into continuous evidence so that we can discover and address security problems," said Dr Allan Friedman, Former Senior Advisor and Strategist, CISA.

stories.title: Nvidia fallout throws spotlight on AI boom in Malaysia and Singapore
stories.summary: The resignation of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang following revelations of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy has intensified US congressional pressure for stricter export controls on AI chips to China. Southeast Asian data center and semiconductor executives now anticipate heightened regulatory scrutiny of chip flows through Singapore and Malaysia, two major hubs for AI infrastructure investment.
stories.why_it_matters: Malaysia and Singapore's status as neutral transit points for AI hardware is now politically contested; data center operators and cloud providers in both countries face potential supply chain disruptions if Washington mandates end-use verification for all advanced GPU shipments. Regional governments must balance attracting foreign hyperscale investment against compliance costs that could divert projects to alternative locations like Indonesia or Vietnam.

stories.title_zh: Nvidia风波将聚光灯投向马来西亚和新加坡的AI热潮
stories.summary_zh: 前Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang因与一名疑似中国间谍有染而辞职，此事加剧了美国国会要求对向中国出口AI芯片实施更严格管制的压力。东南亚的data center和半导体高管现在预期，新加坡和马来西亚这两个AI基础设施投资主要枢纽的芯片流动将面临更严格的监管审查。
stories.why_zh: 马来西亚和新加坡作为AI硬件中立转运点的地位现在受到政治争议；如果华盛顿要求对所有advanced GPU出货进行最终用途验证，两国的data center运营商和cloud providers可能面临供应链中断。地区政府必须在吸引外国hyperscale投资与合规成本之间取得平衡，否则这些成本可能将项目转移到印度尼西亚或越南等替代地点。
stories.content:
SINGAPORE (Nov 13): Southeast Asia's chip and data centre industries expect greater scrutiny after news of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy put the spotlight on Singapore and Malaysia, executives and analysts said.

US lawmakers from both parties are pushing for tougher restrictions on China's access to advanced artificial intelligence chips after the Huang scandal increased scrutiny of Nvidia's role in US national security.

Washington restricts exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to protect US dominance of the sector, but lawmakers want to close a loophole that allows Chinese firms to rent computing power from overseas data centres and access the systems equipped with the chips remotely.

Tougher regulations could include new export rules and licensing requirements to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The alleged spy, Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, was an executive at a cloud computing firm in Singapore called Megaspeed that has subsidiaries in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Australia and the US.

Megaspeed has been under investigation by Singapore authorities since February last year for potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offences.

"After this case, every operator in the chain will be expected to know its end user. Southeast Asian operators will still get Nvidia chips, but proof of where every chip sits and who it serves is now part of the product," said Ke Yan, head of research at Singapore-based investment research firm Shenton Research.

Southeast Asia's data centre industry is thriving. Since 2021, Malaysia has approved RM385.7 billion (US$94.67 billion) of data centre-related investments in the country, according to the trade ministry, while Thailand has 42 data centres, representing 3,400 MW of IT load and about 750 billion baht (US$22.58 billion) in investment as of February.

Indonesia's data centre market was valued at US$2.81 billion in 2025.

Gary Goh, CEO of Malaysia-based data centre consultancy Sprint DC, likened the current situation to a "post-DeepSeek moment". "Once the new rules are out, there will be a lot more restrictions for countries like Malaysia. There could be a short- to medium-term market shock to the Malaysian data centre market," said Goh.

The AI boom has boosted the region, with Singapore in August raising its economic growth forecast to 4.5%-5.5% this year, from 2%-4%, citing the AI cycle. In Malaysia, rising data centre development projects pushed the construction sector up 6% in the third quarter of 2026.

Singapore's and Malaysia's trade ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Malaysia on Thursday said it was weighing a law that will allow the government to monitor data centre operations, including their use of high-performance chips, saying it needed to ensure that any chips subject to US restrictions were imported into Malaysia for domestic use, rather than for re-export.

An investor and CEO of an Asian neocloud company, who declined to be named, spent Friday morning in calls with lawyers in the US. "Everyone is still figuring out... Maybe every time you export something, there will be additional process to go through. We are worried about more scrutiny which will make it longer for chips to come through," the CEO said.

In February 2025, Singapore said that while 22% of Nvidia's chip sales were booked to entities with operations in Singapore only 1% physically came to Singapore. Singapore has also just charged a fifth person in an AI server fraud case.

Jarick Seet, head of small-mid caps at Maybank, said the region could weather tighter rules. "Singapore itself will be more stringent, I think it's a natural thing that happens. Singapore will tighten rules and the US will tighten rules, but I don't think this will harm Singapore's and Malaysia's prospect of buying chips."

A senior executive at a chip maker in Singapore, who declined to be named, even sees a silver lining. "With Jensen out, then the Chinese will have a harder time getting chips from the US. Maybe it is not a bad thing for the non-US people who will have more access to chips."

If the US slows building data centres following Democratic victories in key data-centre states such as Texas and Georgia in midterm elections, "those companies are going to look elsewhere and likely come to countries that can offer them land and deals and power," the executive said. "Even if we lose a chunk of the China business, I think we will get other companies coming looking for compute."

stories.title: Nebius answers the AI financing question with customer prepayments
stories.summary: Nebius Group, an artificial intelligence infrastructure and neocloud company headquartered in Amsterdam, reports that prepayments on its Q3 agreements covered more than 100 percent of the associated capital expenditure, including data center construction and networking, up from 50 to 60 percent in Q2 2026. In its results for Q3 2026, the company also revised its […]
stories.title_zh: Nebius通过客户预付款回应AI融资问题
stories.content:
Nebius Group, an artificial intelligence infrastructure and neocloud company headquartered in Amsterdam, reports that prepayments on its Q3 agreements covered more than 100 percent of the associated capital expenditure, including data center construction and networking, up from 50 to 60 percent in Q2 2026.

In its results for Q3 2026, the company also revised its capex guidance for 2026 to approximately US$ 27 billion, above its previous range of US$ 20 billion to US$ 25 billion, as it invests in capacity for 2027, in particular at its own sites. It expects to reach pre-tax breakeven by the end of 2027.

Arkady Volozh, Nebius Group Chief Executive Officer and founder, told investors that the company expects prepayments and financing against existing contracts with investment-grade customers to cover between 75 and 85 percent of its 2027 capex.

“In recent weeks our industry has been asked questions about how the AI build-out will be financed. Our focus remains on building a healthy, profitable business for the long term. We will continue to invest across the business – in our capacity and infrastructure build-out, in our platform and products, and in the team that takes this to market,” Volozh wrote in a letter to shareholders.

Across its sites, Nebius now has more than 4 GW of capacity contracted and it is on track to have 5 GW of contracted power by the end of the year.The company has also secured exclusive site rights for a planned 100 MW multi-campus AI data center project in Alberta, Canada. The Canada site is expected to come online in 2027, as will a new 50 MW colocation facility in South Carolina, and two colocation facilities in India, the company’s first in the Asia-Pacific region.

The company told shareholders that its asset-light model will contribute “to our ability to expand beyond our own contracted power in a cost-efficient way.”

For the quarter, Nebius reported that revenue had grown 571 percent from US$ 146.1 million in Q3 2025 to US$ 980.8 million. Adjusted EBITDA was US$ 465.8 million against a loss of US$ 5.2 million. Net losses were reduced from US$ 119.6 million to US$ 37.5 million. Revenue for 2026 is now expected to be at the low end of the US$ 3 billion to US$ 3.4 billion range, and 2027 revenue is expected to be between US$ 12 billion and US$ 13 billion.

stories.title: Japanese consortium including Mitsubishi Electric and NTT explores mega-satellite constellation business
stories.summary: Mitsubishi Electric, a Japanese electronics and electrical equipment manufacturer, has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Japanese telecommunications company, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation (NTT), NTT DOCOMO BUSINESS, MUFG Bank and the Development Bank of Japan to explore the development and commercial operation of a large-scale satellite constellation. The agreement covers a coordinated network […]
stories.title_zh: 包括Mitsubishi Electric和NTT在内的日本财团探索巨型卫星星座业务
stories.content:
Mitsubishi Electric, a Japanese electronics and electrical equipment manufacturer, has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Japanese telecommunications company, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation (NTT), NTT DOCOMO BUSINESS, MUFG Bank and the Development Bank of Japan to explore the development and commercial operation of a large-scale satellite constellation.

The agreement covers a coordinated network of satellites designed to support communications, Earth observation, positioning, navigation and timing (PNT), and space-based data centers. According to a press release, the five companies will assess the technical and commercial feasibility of the proposed system, including the infrastructure needed to connect satellites, ground stations, communications networks and operating systems. They will also examine potential services for customers in Japan and overseas, as well as the business framework needed to develop and operate the network.

“In recent years, space development initiatives by both the public and private sectors have accelerated worldwide, driven by technological advances such as the miniaturization and enhanced capabilities of satellites, as well as increased launch frequency. In particular, satellite constellations, in which multiple satellites operate in coordination, are increasingly being utilized as social infrastructure in a wide range of fields, including communications, Earth observation, positioning, disaster prevention and mitigation, and national security. Against this backdrop, further efforts are needed to expand the use of space,” the companies said, explaining the rationale for the move.

Mitsubishi Electric will focus on the constellation’s overall system architecture and integration, drawing on its experience in satellite manufacturing, ground facilities and defense and space systems. The company will also study the use of its Digital Space Interface (DSI), an open interface standard under development with other space companies. DSI is intended to support the installation and updating of large software packages on satellites in orbit, allowing operators to modify services more efficiently.

Potential applications include communications during natural disasters and in areas with limited network coverage, satellite-based positioning services and improved processing of Earth observation data through space-based data centers. The companies will also identify technical requirements and challenges associated with building and operating the proposed infrastructure.

The agreement comes as governments and private companies expand satellite networks, supported by advances in satellite technology and more frequent launches. The five partners aim to develop an open and interoperable system, but have not announced a deployment schedule, investment commitments or a timeline for commercial operations.
